# Flying shuttle and power loom (`power_loom`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/manufacturing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Tools, machines & manufacturing (`manufacturing`)
- Deps: needs treadle_loom, cam_camshaft; helped by spinning_machines, rotative_steam_engine, belt_drive
- Core idea: Flying shuttle: the shuttle runs on small wheels along a ledge on the beater and is knocked from side to side by leather drivers in a box at each end, jerked by a cord in the weaver's hand. One weaver can now make wide cloth alone and about twice as fast. The power loom takes all the motions from one driven shaft: cams lift the shafts, a spring or cam throws the shuttle, a crank swings the beater, a ratchet winds the cloth forward. The real difficulty is what a weaver does without thinking: the loom must stop itself when the weft breaks or runs out and when the shuttle fails to arrive, or it smashes hundreds of warp threads; and the warp must be sized with starch paste beforehand so that it survives the rubbing.
- Pitfalls:
  - No stop motions for a broken weft or a trapped shuttle
  - Unsized warp; the first power looms had to be stopped constantly to dress it
  - Speeding up weaving without more yarn: the flying shuttle made the yarn shortage worse
  - Underrating the resistance: Kay's house was attacked, and weavers broke looms in 1812 and 1826
- History: europe: c. 1580–1604 – multi-ribbon 'engine' looms at Danzig and Leiden, restricted by several towns; 1733 John Kay's flying shuttle; 1745 Vaucanson's automatic loom; 1785–1787 Edmund Cartwright's power loom patents; 1803 Radcliffe and Johnson's warp dressing machine; 1803–1813 Horrocks's loom; 1822 Roberts's iron power loom; americas: 1814 – Francis Cabot Lowell's power loom at Waltham; 1894 Northrop's automatic weft-replenishing loom; east_asia: 1924 – Sakichi Toyoda's automatic loom with shuttle change, Japan
- Read:
  - Richard L. Hills, Power in the Industrial Revolution (1970)
